entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Kanhopatra (c. 1420–1488 CE) stands as a singular figure in the 15th-century Marathi Bhakti movement, revered as one of the few female saint-poets within the Varkari sampradaya, a devotional sect primarily focused on the worship of Vitthal (Vithoba) at Pandharpur. Born into a community of courtesans in Mangalwedha, Maharashtra, her life diverged sharply from societal expectations, illustrating the profound democratizing and inclusive potential of the Bhakti tradition. Her journey from the courtly life to intense spiritual devotion challenged established social hierarchies, making her a powerful symbol of spiritual liberation accessible to all, irrespective of birth or status. Her unique background and steadfast devotion continue to resonate deeply within the spiritual landscape of South Asia.

Kanhopatra's primary contribution lies in her poignant abhangas, devotional poems addressed directly to Vitthal. These compositions, numbering around thirty, articulate her yearning for divine union, her struggles with societal pressures, and her unwavering faith, often using the metaphor of a bride longing for her beloved. Unlike many male Bhakti saints who renounced worldly life, Kanhopatra's spiritual path was forged within her challenging circumstances, transforming her vulnerability into a source of profound spiritual expression. Her most famous abhanga, 'Nako Devaraya Antar Ata' ('O God, do not distance me now'), captures her fervent plea for divine grace and protection, culminating in her legendary self-surrender at the feet of Vitthal in Pandharpur.
